findings.why: "At the discretion of" is the fixed English idiom, so "rests at the discretion of the appointing authority" reads better. "Rest with" is normally followed by a person or body ("the decision rests with the authority"), not with "the discretion of".

Both passives are correct. Older grammar books make the noun object the subject — "Advantage has not been taken of his generosity" — while treating "take advantage of" as one unit gives "His generosity has not been taken advantage of". Two defensible answers.

findings.why: The marked answer is complex, but so is (c) "As he was tired, he fell asleep" — a main clause plus a subordinate clause of reason. The question has two correct options.

The mark stands: with verbs of knowing, the passive takes "to" — "He is known to me" is the idiomatic and usually keyed answer. (a) "He is known by me" is only the mechanical by-agent form some books show.
"He was ill and could not come" is a compound sentence — two main clauses joined by "and". A complex sentence needs a subordinate clause, so the answer is (b) "As he was ill, he could not come."
Both forms are taught. "Two and two make four" treats the two subjects as plural; "makes" is defended by treating the sum as one idea, which is the rule this key follows.
Booklet misprint: options (a) and (d) are printed with identical text. It does not change the answer — (c), with the past perfect "had got", is the correct reported form.
